title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
State Farm's defense lawyers submitted court filings that contained fabricated legal cases, false quotations, and invented legal holdings, created by an AI tool called Irys. The tool generated seven fake case citations across eight filings with incorrect case titles and misquoted material. Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson used the system believing it was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription, and the lead lawyer Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the filings.

This is a failure of a language model to distinguish invented content from real legal precedent, combined with deployment without human verification of citations. The failure occurred in a high-stakes civil litigation setting where false authorities in court filings can mislead judges and opposing counsel. A human review of each case citation against legal databases before filing would have caught every fabrication.

It is not established whether the law firm or individual lawyers faced sanctions, whether the court rejected the filings, or what consequences followed for the plaintiff's case.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that created fake legal cases, false quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit in Los Angeles. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire destroyed her home in Carson. While repairs were underway, water damage from a storm occurred, and Meni-Siliga said State Farm delayed approving repairs, leaving the work incomplete. She subsequently lost her home to foreclosure and declared bankruptcy.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys that generated seven fake case citations across eight filings, incorrect case titles, and misquoted material. She mistakenly believed the tool was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription. Kenneth Katel, the lead lawyer on the case, accepted responsibility for the filings and said the firm updated its AI policy. The incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI. The case is scheduled for trial in October.
